note: Original practice questions written for Patch Notes. They are not real exam questions.

questions.stem: Ransomware encrypts a hospital's patient records so staff can't open them. Which part of the CIA triad is hit most directly?

options.why: The records still exist but nobody can use them: that's a loss of availability.
Confidentiality is about who can read data. Encryption by an attacker stops everyone reading it; it doesn't by itself reveal it (though many gangs also steal data).
Integrity is about data being changed without authorisation. The main effect here is that the data can't be used at all.
Non-repudiation is about proving who did something, such as with a digital signature.

questions.stem: A vendor publishes a file and its SHA-256 hash on the same web page. What does a matching hash prove to someone who downloads it?

options.text: The file is identical to the one the hash was made from
options.why: A hash is a fingerprint: any change to the file gives a different hash.
A hash says nothing about what's in the file, only whether it changed.

options.text: The file definitely came from the vendor
options.why: If an attacker can change the page, they can change the hash too. Proving origin needs a digital signature.
Hashing isn't encryption; the file is unchanged by being hashed.

questions.stem: Which proves that a software update came from its vendor and wasn't changed on the way?

options.text: A digital signature made with the vendor's private key
options.why: Only the vendor holds the private key, and anyone can check the signature with the public key. It covers both origin and integrity.

options.text: An MD5 checksum next to the download link
options.why: MD5 is broken for this (collisions are practical), and a checksum on the same page proves nothing about who published it.
Encryption keeps it secret; it doesn't prove who made it.

options.text: Downloading it from a fast mirror
options.why: Mirrors are third parties; a signature is what lets you trust their copy.

questions.stem: Why does each stored password get its own random salt?

options.text: So identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless
options.why: With a unique salt, attackers must work on every account separately.

options.text: So the password can be recovered if the user forgets it
options.why: Salted hashes still can't be reversed. Passwords are reset, not recovered.

options.text: So a fast hash such as SHA-256 becomes safe for passwords
options.why: A salt doesn't slow each guess down. Password storage also needs a slow function such as Argon2id or bcrypt.
A salt is stored next to the hash in the clear; it isn't a key.

questions.stem: Which statement about symmetric encryption, such as AES, is true?

options.text: The same key encrypts and decrypts, so both sides need a safe way to share it
options.why: That's why protocols such as TLS use asymmetric cryptography first, to agree a shared key.

options.text: It uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt
options.why: That's asymmetric encryption (RSA, elliptic curve).

options.text: It's much slower than asymmetric encryption
options.why: The opposite: symmetric encryption is fast, which is why it protects the bulk of the data.

options.text: It can't be used for large files
options.why: It's what disk encryption and VPNs use for large amounts of data.

questions.stem: Why should a new system not use SHA-1 to sign documents or certificates?

options.text: Researchers have shown it's practical to create two different files with the same SHA-1 hash
options.why: That's a collision (the SHAttered attack, 2017). A signature on one file would also fit the other.

options.text: SHA-1 hashes can be reversed to recover the original file
options.why: Hashes aren't reversed. The problem is collisions.
Speed isn't the issue; its collision resistance is broken.
SHA-1 is a hash function, not a cipher.

questions.stem: A sign at a site entrance says the area is watched by CCTV. What type of control is the sign mainly?

options.why: Its job is to discourage someone from trying in the first place.
Corrective controls fix things after an incident, such as restoring from backup.
A compensating control stands in for one that can't be used.
A sign is a physical control. (The cameras themselves are detective.)

questions.stem: What is the core idea of zero trust?

options.text: Don't trust anything because of where it is on the network: verify every request using identity, device and context
options.why: Being 'inside' no longer earns trust; every access is checked.

options.text: Trust everything inside the firewall and nothing outside
options.why: That's the old perimeter model zero trust replaces.

options.text: Block all access to the internet
options.why: Zero trust is about verifying access, not cutting it off.

options.text: Remove passwords and rely on the firewall
options.why: Strong identity checks are central to zero trust.

questions.stem: Which gives non-repudiation for an email?

options.text: A digital signature made with the sender's private key
options.why: Only the sender could have produced it, so they can't credibly deny sending it.
TLS protects the message in transit; it doesn't prove who wrote it.

options.text: A hash of the message in the subject line
options.why: Anyone can compute a hash. It proves nothing about the author.
A read receipt shows it was opened, not who sent it.

questions.stem: Your browser trusts the certificate for shop.example.com. Who vouched that the public key in it belongs to that site?

options.text: The certificate authority (CA) that signed the certificate
options.why: The CA checked the site controls the name, then signed the certificate. Your browser trusts the CA because its root certificate is in the device's trust store.

options.text: The website, by signing it with its own private key
options.why: Anyone can sign their own certificate; that's a self-signed certificate, and browsers warn about it because nobody independent vouched for it.

options.text: The DNS server that gave the site's IP address
options.why: DNS only maps names to addresses. It says nothing about who owns a key.

options.text: The TLS session key agreed during the handshake
options.why: Session keys encrypt the connection after the certificate has already been checked; they don't prove identity.

questions.stem: A web server's private key has been stolen. What should happen to its certificate?

options.text: Revoke it, then issue a new certificate for a newly generated key pair
options.why: Revocation tells clients to stop trusting the old certificate, and a new key pair means the stolen key is useless for the replacement.

options.text: Renew it early with the same key pair
options.why: The thief still holds that private key, so a renewed certificate with the same key is just as compromised.

options.text: Leave it until it expires, then replace it
options.why: Until then the attacker could impersonate the server to anyone they can intercept.
Worth doing if the server was breached, but it does nothing about a key that's already been copied.

questions.stem: Which protocol lets a client ask about the revocation status of one certificate, instead of downloading a whole list?

options.why: The client (or the server, with OCSP stapling) gets a signed good, revoked or unknown answer for that one certificate.
A CRL is the whole list of revoked serial numbers that the client downloads and searches.
A CSR is what you send a CA to ask for a certificate in the first place.
SCEP is a protocol for enrolling devices to get certificates, not for checking revocation.

questions.stem: An administrator needs a certificate for a new web server. What do they send to the certificate authority?

options.text: A certificate signing request (CSR) with the public key and the server's name
options.why: The CSR carries the public key and the identity to put in the certificate. The private key stays on the server.

options.text: The server's private key, so the CA can sign it
options.why: The private key should never leave the server. The CA only needs the public key.
The CA already has that; it's what browsers use to check certificates the CA issues.
That's for listing revoked certificates, not requesting new ones.

questions.stem: A company buys a wildcard certificate for *.example.com. Which name does it cover?

options.why: The * matches exactly one label to the left of example.com.
A wildcard doesn't match the bare domain, so certificates usually list it as an extra name too.
The * stands for one label only, so it doesn't reach two levels down.
That's a different domain altogether.

questions.stem: Why do certificate authorities sign website certificates with an intermediate CA instead of their root CA?

options.text: The root's private key can stay offline; if an intermediate is compromised it can be revoked without replacing the root on every device
options.why: Roots are built into operating systems and browsers, so they are hard to replace. Keeping them offline and using intermediates limits the damage of a breach.

options.text: Intermediate certificates use stronger encryption than roots
options.why: Strength depends on the key type and size, not on where the certificate sits in the chain.

options.text: Browsers can't check a root CA's signature
options.why: They can: every chain is checked up to a trusted root.

options.text: It lets the website skip sending its own certificate
options.why: The server still sends its certificate, usually along with the intermediate.

questions.stem: A firewall rule blocks inbound RDP from the internet. Which control category and type is it?

options.why: It's enforced by technology, and it stops the connection before anything happens.
Detective controls notice and record events, like an IDS alert. This rule blocks them.
Physical controls are things like locks and fences.
Managerial controls are policies and risk decisions; this is a rule enforced by a device.

questions.stem: An intrusion detection system (IDS) raises an alert when it sees a known attack pattern, but lets the traffic through. What type of control is it?

options.why: It spots and reports the activity; someone or something else has to act on it.
That would be an intrusion prevention system (IPS), which can block the traffic.
Corrective controls fix things afterwards, such as restoring from backup.
Deterrents discourage attempts, like a warning banner; an attacker usually can't even see an IDS.

questions.stem: An old machine can't run the company's endpoint protection, so it's moved to an isolated network segment with strict firewall rules and extra monitoring. What type of control is this?

options.why: It reduces the risk in a different way when the normal control can't be used.
Nothing has gone wrong yet; corrective controls fix things after an incident.
Directive controls tell people what to do, such as a policy.
It's not there to discourage anyone; it limits what an attacker could reach.

questions.stem: Every new member of staff must read and sign an acceptable use policy. Which control category and type is it?

options.why: It's set by management and tells people what they must and mustn't do.
A signed policy doesn't technically stop anything.
Detective controls find events after they happen, like log reviews.
Physical controls are things like fences, locks and guards.

questions.stem: Which two are technical controls? (Choose two.)

options.why: Enforced by the sign-in system itself.
Enforced by software on the device.
That's an operational control: people do it, and it relies on them.

options.text: A fence around the data centre
options.why: That's a physical control.

questions.stem: Someone phones the finance team pretending to be the managing director and demands an urgent payment. What is this?

options.why: Voice phishing: social engineering over the phone, often with urgency and authority.
Smishing is phishing by text message (SMS).
That compromises a website the targets are known to visit.
Typosquatting registers lookalike domain names.

questions.stem: Sign-in logs show one address trying a single common password against hundreds of different accounts, slowly. What is this?

options.why: One password, many accounts, slowly: it avoids the lockouts that many guesses on one account would trigger.

options.text: A brute force attack on one account
options.why: That tries many passwords against one account.
Credential stuffing replays username and password pairs leaked from other sites.
Rainbow tables are precomputed hashes used against a stolen password database, not live sign-ins.

questions.stem: Typing a single quote (') into a website's login form returns a database error. What does this most suggest?

options.text: The input reaches a database query unsafely: a possible SQL injection flaw
options.why: The quote broke the query's syntax. Parameterised queries prevent this.
XSS is about scripts running in other users' browsers, not database errors.
One request causing an error message isn't a denial of service.
The error comes from how the input is handled, not its length.

questions.stem: A forum lets someone post a comment containing a script that then runs in every visitor's browser. What is this?

options.why: The script is saved on the site and served to everyone. Output encoding prevents it.
SQL injection attacks the database through a query, not other users' browsers.
Reflected XSS bounces the script straight back in one response, usually via a crafted link; this one is stored.
SSRF makes the server send requests on the attacker's behalf.

questions.stem: What best limits the damage of a ransomware attack?

options.text: Offline or immutable backups that are regularly tested by restoring them
options.why: If you can restore, you don't depend on the attackers. Untested backups often fail when needed.
Paying doesn't guarantee recovery, funds crime, and may break sanctions rules.
Antivirus helps, but new ransomware often isn't detected at first.

options.text: Backups on a share the same users can write to
options.why: Ransomware encrypts every share it can reach, including that one.

questions.stem: What is a zero-day vulnerability?

options.text: A flaw that attackers exploit before a fix is available
options.why: Defenders have had 'zero days' to patch, so other controls matter.

options.text: A flaw fixed on the day it was reported
options.why: That describes a fast patch, not a zero-day.

options.text: A vulnerability with a CVSS score of zero
options.why: CVSS scores have nothing to do with the name.

options.text: Malware that deletes itself after one day
options.why: That's not what the term means.

questions.stem: Attackers compromise a widely used software library's update, so every application that installs it gets malware. What is this?

options.why: Attacking a trusted supplier reaches all of its customers at once.
That compromises a website the targets visit.
On-path attacks intercept traffic between two parties.
DDoS overwhelms a service; it doesn't plant code.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest sign that an account has been taken over?

options.text: A successful sign-in from a new country right after many failures, followed by a change to the MFA settings
options.why: Failures then success suggests guessing; changing MFA is how attackers keep access.

options.text: The user forgot their password once this month
options.why: Ordinary and harmless on its own.

options.text: A sign-in at 9am from the usual office
options.why: That's normal behaviour.

options.text: A password change forced by policy
options.why: Expected and explained by the policy.

questions.stem: Why put guest Wi-Fi in its own VLAN, with firewall rules between it and the office network?

options.text: So guest devices can't reach internal systems, even though they share the same switches
options.why: Segmentation keeps untrusted devices away from what matters.
Segmentation is about separation, not speed.
VLAN tags aren't encryption.

options.text: So guests don't need a Wi-Fi password
options.why: Wireless security is separate from VLANs.

questions.stem: Where should a public web server be placed?

options.text: In a screened subnet (DMZ), separated by firewalls from both the internet and the internal network
options.why: If it's compromised, the attacker still has to get through another firewall to reach internal systems.

options.text: On the internal network next to the file servers
options.why: A compromise would put the attacker right beside your internal systems.

options.text: On the same VLAN as the domain controllers
options.why: That puts your most exposed server next to your most important ones.
Not a hosting location, and it mixes risk badly.

questions.stem: A company rents virtual machines from a cloud provider (IaaS). Who patches the operating system inside those VMs?

options.why: In IaaS the provider secures the physical hardware and hypervisor; the customer secures everything inside the VM.
Not in IaaS. With SaaS the provider manages far more.

options.text: Nobody: cloud VMs don't need patching
options.why: They need patching like any other server.
The hypervisor doesn't manage guest operating systems.

questions.stem: A laptop has full-disk encryption. When does this protect the data?

options.text: At rest: if the laptop is lost or stolen while switched off
options.why: Without the key, the disk is unreadable.
Data in transit needs TLS or a VPN.

options.text: While the user is logged in and malware is running as them
options.why: Once unlocked, the operating system reads the data normally, and so can malware.

options.text: When the files are emailed to someone
options.why: Emailed copies leave the encrypted disk.

questions.stem: A business runs two firewalls as an active-passive pair. Which security goal does this mainly support?

options.why: If one fails, the other takes over.
Two firewalls don't hide data any better than one.
Nothing to do with proving who did what.
Redundancy is about staying up, not preventing changes.

questions.stem: Factory control systems (OT) often can't be patched quickly. What is the usual way to protect them in the meantime?

options.text: Segment them from the office network and the internet, and tightly control what can reach them
options.why: Isolation limits who can reach a vulnerable system while patches are tested for safety.

options.text: Nothing: OT systems can't be attacked
options.why: Attacks on OT are well documented.

options.text: Connect them to the internet for faster updates
options.why: That increases exposure.
Impractical and unnecessary.

questions.stem: An administrator manages switches with Telnet. What should replace it?

options.why: SSH encrypts the session, including the password.
FTP transfers files and also sends passwords in the clear.
Unencrypted too, and not a remote shell.
SNMPv1 uses plain-text community strings; it's not a replacement for a shell.

questions.stem: What does the principle of least privilege mean?

options.text: Each account gets only the access its job needs, and no more
options.why: Less access means less damage if the account is misused or compromised.

options.text: Everyone in IT gets administrator rights
options.why: The opposite of least privilege.

options.text: Passwords must be as short as possible
options.why: Nothing to do with privilege.

options.text: Only the least senior staff can have accounts
options.why: It's about access levels, not seniority.

questions.stem: Which line from a Linux server's /var/log/auth.log shows that an attacker got in?

options.text: Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.45 port 52018 ssh2
options.why: 'Accepted' means the login succeeded.

options.text: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.45 port 51122 ssh2
options.why: A failure: someone tried and was refused.
The username doesn't exist, so nothing got in.

options.text: Connection closed by authenticating user root 203.0.113.45 port 51122 [preauth]
options.why: The connection ended before any login succeeded.

questions.stem: You confirm that an attacker is logged in to a server. Which incident response step comes before removing their tools?

options.why: Stop the damage spreading first (isolate, end sessions, lock accounts), then eradicate.
That comes at the end.
Recovery follows eradication.
Preparation happens before any incident.

questions.stem: What does a SIEM mainly do?

options.text: Collect and correlate logs from many systems, and raise alerts
options.why: It brings sign-ins, servers, firewalls and more into one place so patterns show up.
That's an intrusion prevention system (IPS) or firewall.
That's a vulnerability scanner.
That's a certificate authority.

questions.stem: An 'impossible travel' alert fires because a user appears in two countries 17 minutes apart. The company's VPN exit recently moved abroad. What is the alert?

options.text: A false positive: the activity is legitimate
options.why: The rule saw two locations, but both were the user; the VPN explains it. Check before escalating.

options.text: A true positive needing account lockout
options.why: Locking out a legitimate user causes harm for no gain.
A false negative is a real attack that raised no alert.
Nothing suggests leaked passwords from other sites.

questions.stem: An attacker guessed a user's VPN password and then created their own admin account on a server. Which containment is most complete?

options.text: Lock the new admin account and end its sessions, reset the stolen password and end its sessions, and block the attacker's address
options.why: That removes both ways back in, plus the source.
They already have a password and an account; they can come from another address.
That destroys evidence and fixes nothing.
The accounts survive a reboot.

questions.stem: An email appears to come from your bank, but its headers show SPF fail and DKIM fail. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it as spoofed: don't click anything, and report it
options.why: Both checks failing means the bank's domain didn't send it.

options.text: Trust it because the logo looks right
options.why: Logos are easy to copy.

options.text: Reply to ask whether it's genuine
options.why: You'd be asking the attacker.

options.text: Forward it to colleagues to check
options.why: That spreads the risk.

questions.stem: Which should be patched first?

options.text: A flaw on an internet-facing VPN appliance that is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list
options.why: It's exposed and already being exploited: likelihood and impact are both high.

options.text: A CVSS 9.8 flaw in a test system with no network access and no known exploitation
options.why: A high score, but much less likely to be attacked.

options.text: A low-severity flaw in a desktop calculator app
options.why: Low impact and low likelihood.
Age isn't risk. Exploitation and exposure are.

questions.stem: Which kind of multi-factor authentication best resists phishing?

options.text: A FIDO2 security key or passkey
options.why: It's bound to the real site's domain, so a fake site can't use it.
Users can be tricked into typing it into a fake site, and SIM swaps can intercept it.
Also easy to phish, and depends on the mailbox's security.
Answers are often guessable or findable online.

questions.stem: Which change does most to stop SSH password guessing from succeeding?

options.why: Without passwords there's nothing to guess.
A banner changes the message people see; guesses work exactly as before.

options.text: Log failed attempts in more detail
options.why: Better visibility, but it doesn't stop a guess working.
Unrelated to guessing.

questions.stem: A company buys cyber insurance. Which risk response is this?

options.why: Part of the financial impact moves to the insurer.
Acceptance means living with the risk as it is.
Avoidance stops the risky activity altogether.
Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact with controls.

questions.stem: Leadership decides that a small risk in a legacy app costs more to fix than to live with, and records the decision. Which risk response is this?

options.why: A documented, owned decision to accept a known risk.
Nothing is passed to a third party.
The app is still in use.
No control is being added.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?

options.text: A policy says what must happen; a procedure gives the step-by-step how
options.why: For example, the policy says all laptops are encrypted; the procedure explains how to set it up.
They sit at different levels.

options.text: A procedure is legally binding and a policy is optional
options.why: Neither statement is generally true.

options.text: Policies are written by IT, procedures by HR
options.why: Ownership varies; the difference is purpose.

questions.stem: What does a recovery time objective (RTO) set?

options.text: The longest acceptable time to restore a service after a disruption
options.why: How long the business can be without it.

options.text: The most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose
options.why: That's the recovery point objective (RPO).
That's retention.

options.text: The time to detect an incident
options.why: That's a detection measure, often called mean time to detect.

questions.stem: A system has a recovery point objective (RPO) of one hour. Which backup approach meets it?

options.text: Backups or replication at least every hour
options.why: You can never lose more than an hour of data.
Up to 24 hours of data could be lost.
Up to a week of data could be lost.
That's an RTO, not an RPO.

questions.stem: Before a supplier is given access to customer data, what matters most?

options.text: Assess the supplier's security and put requirements in the contract, such as a data processing agreement
options.why: Third-party risk is managed by checking first and agreeing obligations in writing.

options.text: Trust them because they're a well-known brand
options.why: Big names have breaches too.

options.text: Give them full access so they can work quickly
options.why: Least privilege applies to suppliers as well.

options.text: Nothing, as long as they're in the same country
options.why: Location doesn't replace due diligence.

questions.stem: Under UK GDPR, a personal data breach that's likely to put people's rights at risk must be reported to the ICO how quickly?

options.text: Without undue delay, and where feasible within 72 hours of becoming aware of it
options.why: Article 33 of UK GDPR sets the 72-hour expectation.

options.text: Within 24 hours of the breach happening
options.why: The law says 72 hours, counted from when the organisation becomes aware.
Far too slow under UK GDPR.

options.text: Only if the press finds out
options.why: Reporting is a legal duty, not a reaction to publicity.

questions.stem: Which security awareness approach works best against phishing?

options.text: Short regular training, simulated phishing with feedback, and an easy way to report suspicious emails
options.why: Practice and easy reporting build habits; reports also give the SOC early warning.
People forget, and the threats change.
Fear stops people reporting mistakes, which is when it matters most.
Usually impossible for a business, and phishing also arrives by text and phone.

questions.stem: A firewall change is approved for Saturday night. What should be written down before it starts, in case it goes wrong?

options.text: A backout plan: the exact steps to put the old configuration back
options.why: If the change breaks something, a tested way back limits the outage.

options.text: The names of everyone who uses the network
options.why: That isn't what makes a change safe to undo.

options.text: A new password for the firewall
options.why: Unrelated to undoing a change.

options.text: Nothing: changes can be undone from memory
options.why: Under pressure at night, memory fails. Change management writes it down first.

questions.stem: Why does a change advisory board review a change before it's made?

options.text: To check its impact, risk and timing, and that the right people know about it
options.why: Approval is about understanding what could break and planning around it, such as a maintenance window.

options.text: To make changes slower on purpose
options.why: Delay isn't the goal; avoiding unplanned outages and security gaps is.

options.text: Because only the board can type the commands
options.why: Technical staff make the change; the board approves it.
Review complements testing; it doesn't replace it.

questions.stem: A group defaces a company's website with a political message after the company announced a controversial decision. Which threat actor fits best?

options.why: Their motive is a cause or a message, not money.
Criminal groups are usually after money, such as ransoms or fraud.
Nation-states usually want long-term, quiet access for espionage, not public defacement.
Shadow IT is staff using unapproved technology, not an attack.

questions.stem: A departing employee copies the customer list to a personal cloud account the day before leaving. What is this?

options.why: Someone with legitimate access misusing it. Monitoring data movement and removing access promptly both help.
That compromises a supplier to reach its customers.
No software flaw was used: the access was already theirs.
Nothing was made unavailable.

questions.stem: A new smart camera is put on the office network with its default admin password unchanged. Why is this a risk?

options.text: Default passwords are published online, so anyone who can reach the camera can log in
options.why: Default credentials are one of the most common ways into IoT devices. Change them before connecting.

options.text: It makes the camera's video blurry
options.why: Passwords don't affect image quality.

options.text: Cameras can't use passwords at all
options.why: They can, and they should have strong unique ones.

options.text: It's only a risk if the camera is outdoors
options.why: Where it's mounted doesn't matter: what matters is who can reach it on the network.

questions.stem: A server that normally talks only to the office starts contacting an unknown internet address every 60 seconds, exactly. What does this most suggest?

options.text: Malware beaconing to a command-and-control server
options.why: Regular, automatic check-ins to an unknown address are a classic sign of command and control.
Backups go to known destinations on a schedule, not every minute to an unknown address.

options.text: Someone browsing the web from the server
options.why: People don't connect at precise 60-second intervals.
NTP talks to known time servers, and not this often.

questions.stem: Which control stops unknown programs, including new malware, from running at all on a kiosk PC?

options.why: Only approved programs can run, so anything new is blocked by default.
Signatures only catch malware that's already known.
Passwords don't control which programs run.
Storage has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: A laptop is confirmed to have ransomware. What should happen first?

options.why: Isolation stops the ransomware spreading to shares and other machines while you investigate.
Paying funds crime and doesn't guarantee recovery; containment comes first.
That destroys evidence you may need, and doesn't stop spread that's already started.

options.text: Email everyone a warning from the infected laptop
options.why: Using the infected machine risks spreading the infection.

questions.stem: A test database needs realistic data, but must not contain real customers' card numbers. Which technique fits?

options.text: Data masking: replace the real values with realistic fake ones
options.why: Testers get data that looks right, with nothing real to leak.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the test server
options.why: Encryption protects data at rest, but anyone using the system still sees the real numbers.
A hash proves integrity; it doesn't hide the values from users.

options.text: Moving the database to a faster server
options.why: Speed doesn't protect data.

questions.stem: Why should at least one copy of backups be offline or immutable?

options.text: So ransomware, or an attacker with admin access, can't encrypt or delete it
options.why: Attackers target backups first. A copy they can't reach or change is what lets you recover.

options.text: Because offline backups are faster to restore
options.why: They're often slower; their value is that they survive the attack.
That isn't the security reason.

options.text: Because online backups can't be encrypted
options.why: They can; the point is that attackers can't reach the offline copy.

questions.stem: Staff use company phones for email. Which tool lets IT enforce a screen lock, encryption and remote wipe on them?

options.why: MDM applies and enforces security settings on enrolled devices, and can wipe a lost one.
A VPN protects traffic, not the device's settings.
A SIEM collects and correlates logs; it doesn't configure phones.
That spreads web traffic across servers.

questions.stem: Why does a vulnerability management programme start with an accurate asset inventory?

options.text: You can't patch or protect devices and software you don't know you have
options.why: Unknown assets go unscanned and unpatched, which is how many breaches start.
The value is security, not paperwork.

options.text: It replaces the need for scanning
options.why: The inventory tells you what to scan; it doesn't replace scanning.
An inventory doesn't change performance.

questions.stem: Old laptops are being given to a charity. What must happen to their drives first?

options.text: Securely sanitise or destroy them, and keep a record (certificate) that it was done
options.why: Deleting files or reformatting can leave data recoverable. Sanitisation and a record prove it's gone.

options.text: Delete the user's files and empty the recycle bin
options.why: Deleted files can often be recovered.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the passwords are changed
options.why: Passwords don't stop someone reading the drive directly.
A quick format leaves the data on the disk.

questions.stem: Why do credentialed vulnerability scans find more than non-credentialed ones?

options.text: They log in and check installed software and settings from inside, not just what's visible over the network
options.why: An outside view misses missing patches and weak settings that only show up once logged in.
Speed isn't the reason; depth is.

options.text: They're allowed to exploit the vulnerabilities
options.why: Scanning, with or without credentials, checks for weaknesses; it doesn't exploit them.

options.text: They don't need the system to be switched on
options.why: The system must be running either way.

questions.stem: Analysts are ignoring a SIEM rule because it fires hundreds of times a day on normal activity. What's the right fix?

options.text: Tune the rule to cut false positives, so its alerts mean something again
options.why: Alert fatigue makes real attacks easy to miss. Tuning keeps detection useful.
That removes detection altogether.

options.text: Hire more analysts to read every alert
options.why: That treats the symptom, not the noisy rule.

options.text: Turn off logging on the servers
options.why: Then there's nothing to investigate.

questions.stem: Which control stops staff browsers reaching known malicious websites, whatever device they're on?

options.text: DNS filtering or a secure web gateway
options.why: It blocks lookups or requests for known bad sites before a connection is made.
That protects stored data, not browsing.
That controls who joins the Wi-Fi, not where they browse.
Unrelated to security.

questions.stem: Staff sign in once and get into email, HR and expenses without signing in again. What is this?

options.text: Single sign-on (SSO), often using SAML or OpenID Connect
options.why: One trusted sign-in is shared with the other apps, so there are fewer passwords to steal.
Reuse is the same password typed into many sites; SSO is one sign-in that apps trust.
MFA is about how many factors you prove, not how many apps you reach.
A VPN connects networks; it doesn't sign you in to apps.

questions.stem: What is a main security benefit of automating routine tasks such as disabling a leaver's accounts?

options.text: It happens the same way every time, quickly, without being forgotten
options.why: Consistency and speed reduce mistakes, like an account left active for weeks.

options.text: It removes the need for any security team
options.why: People still design, check and handle exceptions.

options.text: It makes every system immune to attack
options.why: Automation reduces errors; it doesn't remove all risk.

options.text: It hides activity from the logs
options.why: Good automation is logged like anything else.

questions.stem: A SOC tool automatically isolates a laptop and opens a ticket when malware is confirmed. What is this?

options.text: A SOAR playbook (security orchestration, automation and response)
options.why: SOAR runs agreed response steps automatically, so analysts start from a contained situation.
A honeypot is a decoy to attract attackers.
DLP watches for sensitive data leaving.
Scanning finds weaknesses; it doesn't respond to incidents.

questions.stem: Why is a chain of custody kept for evidence from an incident?

options.text: To show who handled it and when, so it can be trusted and used in court
options.why: Gaps in custody let others argue the evidence was altered.
It's about trust in the evidence, not speed.

options.text: Because evidence must be deleted after a week
options.why: Evidence is kept as long as it's needed.

options.text: To decide the severity of the incident
options.why: Severity is assessed separately.

questions.stem: You need to know which program started on a laptop just before suspicious traffic began. Which data source shows it?

options.text: Endpoint logs or EDR (process start events)
options.why: Endpoint telemetry records processes as they launch, with their parent and command line.
These show connections, not which program on the laptop made them.
That shows which address the laptop had, not what ran on it.
They show who entered, not what ran on a computer.

questions.stem: Who decides how sensitive a set of business data is and who may access it?

options.text: The data owner, usually a senior business manager
options.why: The owner is accountable for the data and decides its classification and access.
Custodians look after the data day to day, following the owner's decisions.

options.text: Any member of staff who uses it
options.why: Users follow the rules; they don't set them.
The provider hosts it; the organisation remains responsible.

questions.stem: A tester is given network diagrams and admin credentials before a test. What kind of test is this?

options.why: Full information lets testers go deep quickly. Unknown-environment (black box) testers start with nothing.
In black box testing the tester isn't given internal details.
A scan is automated; this is a test with insider knowledge.
An audit checks compliance against a standard, not by testing attacks.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between an internal audit and an external audit?

options.text: Who does it: the organisation's own staff, or an independent outside party
options.why: External audits give independent assurance, often required by regulators or customers.

options.text: Internal audits only check the network inside the office
options.why: Internal refers to who audits, not where.
They can cover anything in scope.
Independence is the difference, and it matters.
